findings.summary: Array date/time OIDs are not covered by RAW_TEXT_OIDS, so timestamp[]/date[]/timestamptz[] columns are still parsed into JS Dates using the Node runtime timezone
findings.evidence: RAW_TEXT_OIDS only contains the scalar types.builtins.DATE (1082), TIMESTAMP (1114) and TIMESTAMPTZ (1184). The array OIDs (_date 1182, _timestamp 1115, _timestamptz 1185) still fall through to getDefaultParser, which parses each element with the same local-timezone-shifting parser the comment on lines 19-20 says it is fixing. For a `timestamp without time zone` array the default parser interprets each naive value as *local* time, so `toCell` (JSON.stringify -> Date#toJSON -> UTC ISO) yields a value shifted by the Node runtime offset — exactly the bug the change claims to remove, still present for array columns. Also produces an inconsistent cell rendering (raw pg text for scalars, JSON ISO array for arrays).

findings.summary: `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` silently changes the semantics of user queries, not just output formatting
findings.evidence: Line 144 sets the session TimeZone for every executeQuery. This is not purely a rendering concern: `now()`, `current_date`, `date_trunc('day', tstz_col)`, `tstz AT TIME ZONE ...` and any grouping/filtering on timestamptz now evaluate in UTC instead of the server's configured default timezone, so previously-correct user queries can return different rows/aggregates after this change. If only display formatting was intended, formatting the value (or setting only DateStyle) would avoid changing query results.

findings.summary: Duplicate 'queries real tables with rows' test: the change adds a new copy but leaves the original in place
findings.evidence: The added test at line 114 and the pre-existing test at line 309 have the identical name and near-identical body (both create/truncate/drop `_test_products`). This looks like an incomplete replacement (merge artifact): the old assertions at lines 358-374 still assert the raw-row shape the new test was rewritten to stop asserting, and both run, doubling the fixture churn against the same table name.

findings.summary: Existing error-path unit test is now vacuous: the mock throws on the new `SET TimeZone` statement before the wrapped query is ever issued
findings.evidence: `client.query.mockImplementation` only special-cases sql starting with 'SET statement_timeout'; everything else throws. After the change, `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` (service line 144) now hits the throwing branch, so the test 'converts query runtime failures to bad request' passes on a failed SET rather than on a failed user query — the intended error path is no longer exercised.

findings.summary: New e2e test's table cleanup is not in a finally block, leaking `_test_products` when an assertion fails
findings.evidence: The added test (lines 114-197) performs its DROP TABLE via `cleanupClient` after the expectations at lines 165-179. Any failed expectation throws first, so the table (and its rows) survives into subsequent runs; later tests only recover because they use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + TRUNCATE. The setup client at 121-141 correctly uses try/finally, so the omission is inconsistent.

mergedFrom.summary: Cleanup query inside `finally` can throw and mask the original test failure
mergedFrom.evidence: `finally { await rawClient.query('DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ...'); await rawClient.end(); }` — if the loop failed because the connection died, the DROP rejects and replaces the real assertion error, and `rawClient.end()` is then skipped, leaking the connection.

findings.summary: Duplicate test: the new `queries real tables with rows` test is added while the identical pre-existing test is left in place
findings.evidence: The diff adds `it('queries real tables with rows', ...)` at line 114 and the original block with the same name still exists at line 309 (`expect(dataResult.rows).toEqual([{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }, ...])`). Both create, TRUNCATE and DROP the same `_test_products` table and assert the same query, with the older copy asserting the pre-change raw shape and the new copy asserting via `toCell`. This looks like an intended replacement that was appended instead — leaving two same-named tests fighting over one fixture table.

findings.summary: Datasource design doc not updated for the new per-connection session settings and custom pg type-parser policy
findings.evidence: `docs/design/sheets/datasource.md` §'Query Execution' enumerates exactly the connection/execution contract this diff changes (statement timeout, wrapping, max rows) but is not amended with the new `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` / `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` session statements, nor with the decision that DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ are returned as raw Postgres text rather than JS `Date` (an intentional, user-visible value-semantics change: timestamptz values are now rendered in UTC regardless of the source DB timezone). Limitation #9 ('No column type mapping') and the medium-term 'Column type awareness' item are the parts the change touches and neither reflects the new behavior.

findings.summary: Generic value→cell-string formatter placed inside a Store implementation file and exported package-wide, then consumed by backend tests
findings.evidence: `toCell` is a general-purpose serialization helper but lives in `store/readonly.ts` (a Store implementation) and is re-exported from `packages/sheets/src/index.ts`. `packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:8` now imports it, so backend datasource assertions are coupled to the sheet engine's display formatting. A small shared formatting module (or asserting raw values in backend and formatting in sheets' own tests) would keep the layering cleaner. No pre-existing equivalent helper was found (grepped for toDisplay/valueToString/toCellValue/stringify), so this is placement, not duplication.

findings.summary: Exhaustive pg built-in type matrix is scope creep beyond the date/time fix, and it enshrines poor cell output for BYTEA/INTERVAL/CIRCLE
findings.evidence: The change's actual behavior fix concerns DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ, but the diff adds a ~50-entry matrix covering every pg built-in in the backend e2e suite, pinning the sheet display of unrelated types. It also locks in outputs like `'{"type":"Buffer","data":[222,173,190,239]}'` for BYTEA and `'{"years":1,"months":2,"days":3}'` for INTERVAL as the expected spreadsheet cell values — JSON dumps of driver internals, which is a product-level gap `toCell` arguably should handle rather than a behavior worth freezing.

findings.summary: Duplicate `it('queries real tables with rows')` — the old copy was left in place next to the new one
findings.evidence: The diff adds a new test at line 114 named 'queries real tables with rows' that is a near-verbatim copy of the pre-existing test still present at line 309 (same table `_test_products`, same CREATE/TRUNCATE/INSERT/DROP, same query). Both now run in the same file with the same name, so a failure report is ambiguous and the same fixture table is created/dropped twice; the older copy also asserts the *old* expectations (`{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }`) while the new one asserts via `toCell`. This looks like an incomplete replace rather than intentional duplication.

findings.summary: Existing assertions weakened by wrapping in `String()`, so they can no longer detect value-type regressions
findings.evidence: `expect(queryResult.rows).toEqual([{ n: 1 }])` was replaced with `expect(String(rows[0].n)).toBe('1')` (lines 111 and 104-111, and similarly line 163 for `table_name`). `String(x)` passes for the number 1, the string '1', and any object whose toString yields '1'. In a PR whose whole point is changing how pg values are decoded into JS, deliberately erasing the JS type from the assertion removes exactly the signal these tests used to give (e.g. an accidental raw-text parser applied to int4 would no longer fail).

findings.summary: New exported `toCell` (and the ReadOnlyStore change that uses it) has no test in the sheets suite; its `Date` branch is exercised nowhere
findings.evidence: `toCell` is a newly exported public API of packages/sheets and is now the conversion used by `ReadOnlyStore.loadQueryResults` (readonly.ts:73). I globbed packages/sheets/test/**/*.test.ts (53 files; store tests are cell-index, find-edge, store) and grepped for `toCell`/`ReadOnlyStore` across packages: the only usages are src/index.ts, readonly.ts, frontend/datasource-view.tsx, and the Postgres-gated backend e2e spec. So the fast sheets vitest lane has zero coverage of it, and all coverage lives in `describeDb(...)`, which is skipped when DATABASE_URL is unset. Worse, the `val instanceof Date` branch is now unreachable in the e2e coverage too, since the new type parser returns DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ as raw strings — no test in the repo passes a Date to toCell.

findings.summary: Unit spec never asserts the new `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` client option or the RAW_TEXT_OIDS parser logic
findings.evidence: datasource.service.spec.ts was updated only to add the two new `SET` statements (nth-calls 2 and 3). The mocked `Client` constructor args are not asserted for the new `types` option, and `datasourceTypeParser`/`RAW_TEXT_OIDS` (the actual behavioural core of this change — DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ returned as raw text, everything else delegated to the default parser) has no unit test at all. It is only covered indirectly by the DATABASE_URL-gated e2e test, so if that lane is skipped the parser change ships with no coverage. A direct unit assertion (parser for TIMESTAMP returns input verbatim, parser for INT4 still parses to number) would be cheap.

findings.summary: `expect(columns[0].dataTypeID).toBe(expectedOid)` in the all-types loop asserts PostgreSQL's own OIDs, not any behaviour of the code under test
findings.evidence: Inside the 'check correct cell values for all pg built-in types' loop the first assertion compares the OID reported by pg for `CREATE TABLE (val <type>)` against `types.builtins.<TYPE>` — i.e. pg-types constants against pg's catalog. It cannot fail for any change in datasource.service.ts and is effectively a self-check of the pg library. The adjacent `toCell(rows[0].val)` assertion is the one carrying real signal; the OID line is padding.

findings.summary: Error-path unit test mock not updated for the new session-setting queries, so it now fails on `SET TimeZone` instead of the query it means to test
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.spec.ts:153-159 — the mock only returns a result for SQL starting with `SET statement_timeout`; every other statement throws 'syntax error at or near "FROM"'. With the new `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` / `SET DateStyle = ...` calls added at datasource.service.ts:144-145, the throw now happens on the second SET, never on the wrapped SELECT. The test still passes (BadRequestException is raised) but no longer exercises the runtime-query-failure path it was written for. Fix belongs in the spec's mock (whitelist any `SET ` prefix).

findings.summary: Duplicate `it('queries real tables with rows')` — the old copy was left in place alongside the new one, and the two tests share the `_test_products` table
findings.evidence: packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts:309 still defines `it('queries real tables with rows', ...)` with the original assertions (`expect(dataResult.rows).toEqual([{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }, ...])` at :370), while the diff adds a second test with the same name at ~:113. Both CREATE/TRUNCATE/DROP the same `_test_products` table in the shared DATABASE_URL database; jest-e2e.json sets maxWorkers=1 so they serialize today, but the duplicate name makes failures ambiguous and the intended replacement clearly did not happen. The stale copy should be removed.

findings.summary: Sheets date formatter does not recognise the new TIMESTAMPTZ raw text form (`2025-06-15 05:30:00+00`) that query cells now carry
findings.evidence: packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/format.ts:24-66 recognises only `YYYY-MM-DD` and `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`; anything else falls through to `new Date(value)` with `hasTime: false` (:62-66), which drops the time component on render. Previously TIMESTAMPTZ arrived as a JS Date and was serialised to an ISO 'Z' string; with the new raw-text parser it arrives as `2025-06-15 05:30:00+00`, matching neither regex. Only bites when a date number-format is applied to a query-result cell, hence medium confidence.

findings.summary: Design doc's Query Execution / ReadOnlyStore sections still describe the old contract (no session settings, no raw-text date parsing, plain String() cell conversion)
findings.evidence: docs/design/sheets/datasource.md:156-172 lists statement timeout, connection timeout, LIMIT wrapping and 'Row 2+: data rows' but records nothing about the new per-connection `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` / `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'`, the custom `getTypeParser` returning DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ as raw text, or the new `toCell` JSON/ISO conversion in packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:32. This file is nested under docs/design/<topic>/ so the link/doc lanes will not flag it.

findings.summary: SQL read-only guard is bypassable: comment stripping ignores string literals, letting a crafted query smuggle extra statements into the interpolated wrapper in executeQuery
findings.evidence:
`validateSelectQuery` strips `--...` to end-of-line BEFORE any string-literal handling (sql-validator.ts:29). A `--` inside a quoted literal therefore deletes the rest of the query from the validator's view, while Postgres keeps it as data. The validated text is then string-interpolated into the executed SQL at datasource.service.ts:148 (`SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`), and pg's `client.query(sql)` with no parameters uses the simple query protocol, which executes multiple `;`-separated statements.

Attacker (any workspace member who can POST /datasources/:id/query) sends:
  query = `SELECT '--' ) AS q ; DROP TABLE t ; SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1`
Validator sees, after comment stripping, only `SELECT '` → first token SELECT (ok), no forbidden keyword (DROP was deleted, ok), one statement (ok) → valid.
Actually sent to Postgres: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT '--' ) AS q ; DROP TABLE t ; SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements, the middle one an arbitrary write/DDL. The same trick works with `/*` inside a literal (line 30) and with any forbidden keyword, so INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/GRANT are all reachable with the datasource's stored credentials. sql-validator.spec.ts has no case for `--` or `/*` inside a string literal. The guard exists and reads as covered, which is why the wrapper at line 148 concatenates rather than parameterizes.

findings.summary: createClient disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`) whenever sslEnabled is set, so "SSL" connections are MITM-able
findings.evidence: Line 202: `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. This line sits in the function the diff modifies (the `types` option is added at line 204). With verification off, an attacker able to intercept the path to the datasource host (or spoof DNS/BGP for a remote managed Postgres) presents any self-signed certificate; the backend then sends the decrypted datasource password (line 201) and receives query results over the attacker's channel. Users enabling the `sslEnabled` toggle get encryption without authentication, i.e. no protection against an active MITM, while the UI implies a secured connection. No CA/verify option is plumbed through anywhere for datasources.

findings.summary: SSRF / internal network probing: datasource host and port are fully user-controlled with no allowlist, and connection errors are returned to the caller as an oracle
findings.evidence: `create`/`update` accept arbitrary `host`/`port` (lines 43-99) and `createClient` connects to them directly (line 196-205, `connectionTimeoutMillis: 10_000`). Any authenticated workspace member can create a datasource pointing at `127.0.0.1`, the backend's own Postgres, or any RFC1918 host and then call POST /datasources/:id/test, whose response body embeds the raw driver error (line 121: `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }`). ECONNREFUSED vs. timeout vs. "password authentication failed" vs. "received invalid response to SSL negotiation" distinguishes closed / filtered / open-Postgres / open-other-service, giving an internal port scanner and host-existence oracle from an internet-facing endpoint. If any internal Postgres trusts host-based auth (`trust`/`peer` for local connections), the attacker also gets read access to it via executeQuery. I traced the reachable path end to end; I could not confirm the deployment actually has a trust-auth internal DB, hence medium.

findings.summary: Raw Postgres error messages are returned verbatim to API clients, leaking schema and server internals
findings.evidence: Line 166-170 wraps the driver error as `new BadRequestException(pgError.message || ...)`, and line 121 returns `(error as Error).message` from testConnection. Postgres messages include table/column names, function signatures, data values in constraint violations, role names and file paths, so an authenticated caller can enumerate the remote schema and server details through error text alone; combined with the interpolated wrapper at line 148 this is a classic error-based extraction channel. Prefer a generic message plus server-side logging.

findings.summary: create/update/remove return the datasource row including the stored password ciphertext, while findOne/findAllByWorkspace deliberately mask it
findings.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (line 66-69) and `findOne` (line 77) replace `password` with '********', but `create` (line 44), `update` (line 95) and `remove` (line 106) return the Prisma record unmodified, and the controller passes those straight to the client (datasource.controller.ts:43, 67, 104, 117). The response therefore exposes the AES-GCM blob `iv:authTag:ciphertext` (crypto.util.ts:37-41) to every workspace member and to anything that logs responses. Not plaintext, but it hands out the encrypted secret and its IV/tag for offline use if DATASOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY ever leaks, and the inconsistent masking suggests the intent was to never emit it. The new e2e assertion at test/database.e2e-spec.ts:72-73 reads the ciphertext shape from the DB, confirming the format.

findings.summary: The 30s statement_timeout set on the session can be cleared from within the user's own SELECT via set_config, weakening the DoS control the diff extends
findings.evidence: Lines 143-145 set `statement_timeout`, `TimeZone` and `DateStyle` as session GUCs, then line 148 executes the user's SELECT on the same session. `set_config` is not blocked by the validator (`\bSET\b` does not match `set_config`, and SET is not in FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS at sql-validator.ts:1-13), so a query such as `SELECT set_config('statement_timeout','0',false), pg_sleep(600)` can clear the timeout inside the same statement and hold a backend connection and a Node request open far past 30s; repeated calls exhaust connections on the target database. Same applies to the newly added TimeZone/DateStyle settings, which a query can silently override before rows are formatted. Enforcing the timeout via the connection options/`options=-c statement_timeout=...` rather than a resettable session SET would close this.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. RAW_TEXT_OIDS (datasource.service.ts:21-25) contains only the scalar DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ builtins; datasourceTypeParser (34-37) dispatches solely on RAW_TEXT_OIDS.has(oid), so array OIDs (_date 1182, _timestamp 1115, _timestamptz 1185) fall through to getDefaultParser, whose pg-types array parser applies the same element-level parseDate and yields JS Date objects. The override is installed by dataTypeID at line 204, which for an array column is the array OID, so the raw-text branch never fires for arrays. `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` (line 144) only affects Postgres' text rendering of timestamptz and does not prevent the client from interpreting naive `timestamp`/`date` element text as local time. toCell (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:32-36) then JSON.stringifies the Date[] (Date#toJSON -> UTC ISO), baking in the Node-runtime offset shift — the exact bug the comment at lines 19-20 claims to fix — and additionally renders arrays as JSON while scalars render as raw pg text (cf. expectations at database.e2e-spec.ts:250-253). No `process.env.TZ`/`TZ=` pinning exists anywhere in the repo to neutralize the shift. Real, unguarded, and a data-correctness defect in this lens's lane.

finding.summary: toCell's JSON.stringify branch can throw or return undefined, breaking the whole grid load
finding.evidence: `if (typeof val === 'object' && val !== null) return JSON.stringify(val);` — JSON.stringify throws TypeError on circular structures and on objects containing BigInt, and returns `undefined` (not a string) when the value has a `toJSON()` returning undefined. A throw inside loadQueryResults' inner loop (readonly.ts:73) aborts the entire result load, leaving the grid half-populated and the index un-rebuilt; the `undefined` case stores a non-string in `Cell.v` despite the declared `string` return type. A try/catch or String() fallback would make it total.

verdict.reason: The quoted line exists (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:34), but the claimed failure is unreachable and its consequence is already contained. toCell is reached only through ReadOnlyStore.loadQueryResults (readonly.ts:73); its sole production caller is datasource-view.tsx:108, whose rows come from executeDataSourceQuery -> res.json() (packages/frontend/src/api/datasources.ts:104-110). Values that crossed a JSON boundary cannot be circular, cannot contain BigInt, and cannot carry a callable toJSON (a JSON "toJSON" key can only hold data), so JSON.stringify on a non-null object there always returns a string — it can neither throw nor yield undefined. The backend likewise returns raw pg rows (datasource.service.ts:127-165, parsers at lines 21-37) that Nest JSON-serializes before the client sees them, so a BigInt/circular value would fail at server serialization, never at readonly.ts:34. Even granting a hypothetical throw, loadQueryResults is inside try/catch in handleExecute (datasource-view.tsx:103-119) which surfaces it as setQueryError rather than crashing, and the stale-index state is non-crashing (getGrid skips undefined at readonly.ts:109-111; findEdge predicate handles undefined at readonly.ts:127-128) with no data loss since ReadOnlyStore is ephemeral and all writes are no-ops. The only other caller is a backend e2e test (database.e2e-spec.ts:175,301) using default pg parser outputs (int8 -> string, Buffer with a defined toJSON, plain interval/circle objects), none of which trigger the claim.

finding.summary: Datasource design doc not updated for the new per-connection session settings and custom pg type-parser policy

verdict.reason: Verified independently: the diff adds a per-connection session policy (`SET TimeZone = 'UTC'`, `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` at datasource.service.ts:144-145) and a custom pg type-parser that returns DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ as raw Postgres text (datasource.service.ts:19-37, wired at :204). The canonical subsystem doc `docs/design/sheets/datasource.md` §Query Execution (lines 156-162) enumerates precisely this connection/execution contract (wrapping, statement timeout, connection timeout, max rows, response fields) and was not amended; Limitation #9 (line 205) and the medium-term "Column type awareness" item (line 221) still describe the pre-change state. I searched wider for a counterexample and found none: a repo-wide markdown grep for DateStyle/TimeZone/typeParser/timestamptz/"raw text" returns no documentation hit (only an unrelated `timezoneId: "UTC"` in an archived Playwright task doc), no datasource task plan exists under docs/tasks/active/, and no other design doc covers datasource query execution. Under this lens's design-doc-discipline rule (CONTRIBUTING.md:13-16, 55-59 — update the existing area doc for non-trivial/behavioral changes), a user-visible value-semantics change left undocumented in the doc section that already specifies that contract is a major fit violation.

samples.summary: SQL read-only guard is bypassable: comment stripping ignores string literals, letting a crafted query smuggle extra statements into the interpolated wrapper in executeQuery
samples.evidence:
`validateSelectQuery` strips `--...` to end-of-line BEFORE any string-literal handling (sql-validator.ts:29). A `--` inside a quoted literal therefore deletes the rest of the query from the validator's view, while Postgres keeps it as data. The validated text is then string-interpolated into the executed SQL at datasource.service.ts:148 (`SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`), and pg's `client.query(sql)` with no parameters uses the simple query protocol, which executes multiple `;`-separated statements.

Attacker (any workspace member who can POST /datasources/:id/query) sends:
  query = `SELECT '--' ) AS q ; DROP TABLE t ; SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1`
Validator sees, after comment stripping, only `SELECT '` → first token SELECT (ok), no forbidden keyword (DROP was deleted, ok), one statement (ok) → valid.
Actually sent to Postgres: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT '--' ) AS q ; DROP TABLE t ; SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three syntactically valid statements, the middle one an arbitrary write/DDL. The same trick works with `/*` inside a literal (line 30) and with any forbidden keyword, so INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/GRANT are all reachable with the datasource's stored credentials. sql-validator.spec.ts has no case for `--` or `/*` inside a string literal. The guard exists and reads as covered, which is why the wrapper at line 148 concatenates rather than parameterizes.

samples.summary: createClient disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`) whenever sslEnabled is set, so "SSL" connections are MITM-able
samples.evidence: Line 202: `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. This line sits in the function the diff modifies (the `types` option is added at line 204). With verification off, an attacker able to intercept the path to the datasource host (or spoof DNS/BGP for a remote managed Postgres) presents any self-signed certificate; the backend then sends the decrypted datasource password (line 201) and receives query results over the attacker's channel. Users enabling the `sslEnabled` toggle get encryption without authentication, i.e. no protection against an active MITM, while the UI implies a secured connection. No CA/verify option is plumbed through anywhere for datasources.

samples.summary: SSRF / internal network probing: datasource host and port are fully user-controlled with no allowlist, and connection errors are returned to the caller as an oracle
samples.evidence: `create`/`update` accept arbitrary `host`/`port` (lines 43-99) and `createClient` connects to them directly (line 196-205, `connectionTimeoutMillis: 10_000`). Any authenticated workspace member can create a datasource pointing at `127.0.0.1`, the backend's own Postgres, or any RFC1918 host and then call POST /datasources/:id/test, whose response body embeds the raw driver error (line 121: `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }`). ECONNREFUSED vs. timeout vs. "password authentication failed" vs. "received invalid response to SSL negotiation" distinguishes closed / filtered / open-Postgres / open-other-service, giving an internal port scanner and host-existence oracle from an internet-facing endpoint. If any internal Postgres trusts host-based auth (`trust`/`peer` for local connections), the attacker also gets read access to it via executeQuery. I traced the reachable path end to end; I could not confirm the deployment actually has a trust-auth internal DB, hence medium.

samples.summary: Raw Postgres error messages are returned verbatim to API clients, leaking schema and server internals
samples.evidence: Line 166-170 wraps the driver error as `new BadRequestException(pgError.message || ...)`, and line 121 returns `(error as Error).message` from testConnection. Postgres messages include table/column names, function signatures, data values in constraint violations, role names and file paths, so an authenticated caller can enumerate the remote schema and server details through error text alone; combined with the interpolated wrapper at line 148 this is a classic error-based extraction channel. Prefer a generic message plus server-side logging.

samples.summary: create/update/remove return the datasource row including the stored password ciphertext, while findOne/findAllByWorkspace deliberately mask it
samples.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (line 66-69) and `findOne` (line 77) replace `password` with '********', but `create` (line 44), `update` (line 95) and `remove` (line 106) return the Prisma record unmodified, and the controller passes those straight to the client (datasource.controller.ts:43, 67, 104, 117). The response therefore exposes the AES-GCM blob `iv:authTag:ciphertext` (crypto.util.ts:37-41) to every workspace member and to anything that logs responses. Not plaintext, but it hands out the encrypted secret and its IV/tag for offline use if DATASOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY ever leaks, and the inconsistent masking suggests the intent was to never emit it. The new e2e assertion at test/database.e2e-spec.ts:72-73 reads the ciphertext shape from the DB, confirming the format.

samples.summary: The 30s statement_timeout set on the session can be cleared from within the user's own SELECT via set_config, weakening the DoS control the diff extends
samples.evidence: Lines 143-145 set `statement_timeout`, `TimeZone` and `DateStyle` as session GUCs, then line 148 executes the user's SELECT on the same session. `set_config` is not blocked by the validator (`\bSET\b` does not match `set_config`, and SET is not in FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS at sql-validator.ts:1-13), so a query such as `SELECT set_config('statement_timeout','0',false), pg_sleep(600)` can clear the timeout inside the same statement and hold a backend connection and a Node request open far past 30s; repeated calls exhaust connections on the target database. Same applies to the newly added TimeZone/DateStyle settings, which a query can silently override before rows are formatted. Enforcing the timeout via the connection options/`options=-c statement_timeout=...` rather than a resettable session SET would close this.

verdict.reason: Verified end-to-end in the repo. validateSelectQuery strips `--` line comments and `/* */` blocks (sql-validator.ts:28-31) with zero string-literal awareness, and does so BEFORE the first-token check (line 38), the forbidden-keyword scan (lines 47-57), and the statement-count check (lines 60-67). The string-stripping regex `'[^']*'` at line 60 only runs for statement counting and cannot recover the deleted text. Tracing the payload `SELECT '--' ) AS q ; DROP TABLE t ; SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1`: the validator sees only `SELECT '`, so first token is SELECT (passes line 39), no forbidden keyword survives, one statement -> {valid:true}. The ORIGINAL dto.query is then interpolated at datasource.service.ts:148 (`SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`) and executed via client.query(wrappedQuery) with no values array (line 150), so pg uses the simple query protocol and runs all three semicolon-separated statements, the middle being arbitrary DDL/DML against the datasource's stored credentials (decrypted at line 201). No compensating control exists: lines 143-145 set only statement_timeout/TimeZone/DateStyle -- no read-only transaction or default_transaction_read_only. The path is reachable by any workspace member: datasource.controller.ts:133-145 guards POST datasources/:id/query with only JwtAuthGuard (line 24) and assertMember (lines 140-143), no role gate, and validateSelectQuery at datasource.service.ts:128 is its sole read-only enforcement. sql-validator.spec.ts:1-49 confirms no test covers a comment marker inside a quoted literal. This is a genuine injection/read-only-bypass vulnerability, critical under the security rubric.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described: datasource.service.ts:202 sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`, disabling TLS peer verification for every SSL-enabled datasource connection. It is reachable via createClient call sites at datasource.service.ts:115 (connection test) and :138 (query execution), and the decrypted password is sent on that unverified channel (line 201). A repo-wide grep confirms no CA/verify option is plumbed anywhere (only occurrence of `rejectUnauthorized`; sslEnabled is a bare boolean in the DTO at datasource.dto.ts:41,83 and schema.prisma:23). The UI advertises the connection as secured (datasource-list.tsx:133 "SSL" badge), so users get encryption without authentication — an active MITM/DNS-spoof yields credential disclosure and query tampering. This is in the Security lens's crypto/auth lane and is a clear weakness (major), so no refutation ground applies.

Any authenticated workspace member can create a datasource pointing at `127.0.0.1`, the backend's own Postgres, or any RFC1918 host and then call POST /datasources/:id/test, whose response body embeds the raw driver error (line 121: `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }`). verdict.reason: The claimed code exists exactly as described. `create`/`update` (datasource.service.ts:43-57, 80-99) persist fully user-controlled `host`/`port`, validated only as a <=253-char string and a 1-65535 int (datasource.dto.ts:17-25, 56-64) — no loopback/RFC1918 allowlist or denylist exists anywhere in the backend (grep for allowlist/isPrivate/127.0.0.1/SSRF returns only unrelated config and test hits). `createClient` (datasource.service.ts:188-206) feeds those values directly to `new Client({host, port, ...})` with a 10s connect timeout, and `testConnection` returns the raw driver error string to the caller (datasource.service.ts:120-121), while `executeQuery` re-throws the raw pg message (datasource.service.ts:166-170). Reachability is confirmed: controller endpoints are guarded only by JwtAuthGuard + assertMember (datasource.controller.ts:33-44, 120-131, 133-145), and workspace.service.ts:14-23 lets any authenticated user create a workspace in which they are owner/member, so every authenticated user reaches the sink. SSRF is explicitly in the Security lens's lane, so it is not out of scope; no guard renders it unreachable.
